input: A cardiac monitor and a diabetes specialist appointment have been requested, but neither result is available, and the cause of the altered-awareness episode remains unconfirmed.

The driver says road signs are readable at the beginning of a shift but become doubled after several hours, particularly when looking toward the right mirror; covering one eye sometimes helps, although he is not certain which eye he covers and the symptom did not occur during today's interview.
A photocopied eye assessment lists right 6/9 and left 6/18 beside the word unaided, with a separate handwritten 6/6 that is not assigned to an eye or clearly labelled as corrected vision.

The driver denies a constant visual problem and says his hearing was considered normal two years earlier, but his supervisor describes missed spoken instructions and hesitation when checking mirrors during the last month.
Updated optometry and audiology reports are pending, and the apparent difference between earlier records and current functional symptoms has not been reconciled.

He also reports difficulty understanding dispatch over the radio despite following quiet conversation in the consulting room, and says his right hearing aid was being repaired when a recent screening was performed.

A phone image contains thresholds of 30, 45 and 55 dB without a complete frequency axis, an identifiable better ear or a clear statement about hearing aids; the nurse cannot derive the required unaided average from it.

The driver restarted blood-pressure treatment ten days ago after running out of tablets and now describes brief grey vision and a swaying sensation when stepping down from the cab; he says he stays aware throughout, but a coworker recalls him leaning against the vehicle without answering immediately.
